summaries.example: Imagine two perfectly matching toy balls. They have the same color, size, and shape. Could they still be two different balls? Duns Scotus said each one might have its own special “thisness”—a feature that makes it that particular ball, even when no ordinary feature separates them.
summaries.summary: Medieval philosophers asked what makes an individual thing different from every other thing. Duns Scotus answered with the idea of haecceity, or “thisness.” A haecceity is not a color, shape, size, or other ordinary quality. It is a special feature that makes a thing this particular individual. Scotus also discussed common natures, such as humanity, which can be shared by many individuals. He thought a common nature explains how people can be the same kind, while a haecceity explains why each person is a distinct individual. Later thinkers changed, defended, or rejected parts of this view. Some said individuality needs no extra feature: a thing is individual simply through itself.
key_ideas: Duns Scotus proposed haecceity as an explanation of why each individual thing is itself.
A thing can share a kind of nature with other things while still being a different individual.
Scotus thought ordinary qualities, matter, or existence alone could not fully explain individuality.
Other medieval thinkers rejected haecceities or said that things are individuals simply through themselves.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic shows how philosophers examine ideas that seem obvious, such as “this object is different from that one.” It also connects questions about sameness, difference, kinds, and identity. The debate helps us notice that sharing qualities does not always settle whether two things are really one or two.

important_terms.definition: The question of what makes one thing one particular thing instead of another thing of the same kind.
A special, non-qualitative “thisness” that makes a thing the particular thing it is.
A feature that can be shared by many things, such as being human or being round.
A feature that tells what kind of thing something is, such as being a dog or a triangle.

questions_to_think_about: If two objects looked exactly alike, what could make them two objects rather than one?
Can a thing be different from another thing without having a different color, shape, or size?
Is saying “it is this thing because it is this thing” a real explanation?

summaries.example: Consider a possible universe containing only two iron spheres that match in every observable quality and relation. If they are still two spheres, then their difference cannot be explained by color, size, temperature, or position. Scotus’s proposal is that each has a haecceity: a non-qualitative individuating constituent that makes it numerically this sphere. A critic may instead say that the spheres are simply distinct, without distinct haecceities.
summaries.summary: The medieval debate over haecceity concerns the source of numerical individuality. Duns Scotus distinguishes a thing’s common nature from the feature that makes it a determinate individual. A common nature, such as humanity, is not numerically one in the same way that an individual human is one; it has a lesser unity that allows it to be instantiated in many particulars. Scotus argues that each particular therefore requires an individual difference, or haecceity, which is non-qualitative and irreducibly particular. It explains both the individual’s indivisibility into subjective parts and its distinction from other particulars. Scotus’s account depends on a realist view of common natures and on a formal distinction between nature and haecceity. Critics object that this adds difficult entities or distinctions. Ockham rejects Scotus’s account of common natures and formal distinction, maintaining that substances are singular through themselves. The entry also surveys later Scotists, revisions, and modern ideas of “thisness,” which need not treat haecceities as real constituents.
key_ideas: Scotus separates two problems: explaining why a nature can be instantiated many times and explaining why each instance is an indivisible, numerically distinct individual.
His common-nature theory gives a shared nature a real but non-numerical unity; its haecceity supplies determinate individuality.
The haecceity is not a bare substrate with all qualities removed. Scotus treats it as a constituent somewhat like a form, though unlike a qualitative form.
Scotus rejects individuation by accidental qualities, existence alone, or matter alone, because these either depend on the individual or fail to explain individuality adequately.
Ockham and other critics challenge Scotus’s common natures and formal distinction. Some hold that substances are singular through themselves, a position that still functions as a kind of haecceitism.
Later thinkers accepted, revised, or rejected haecceities, showing that the debate concerned both individuation and the status of universals.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue reaches beyond medieval terminology. It asks whether identity can be explained by observable qualities, by shared kinds, by material parts, or by something uniquely particular. It also illustrates a recurring philosophical choice: posit additional metaphysical structure to explain a phenomenon, or accept individuality as basic. The haecceity debate therefore links theories of universals, identity, individuation, and the limits of explanation.

important_terms.definition: The metaphysical problem of explaining why a particular is one indivisible individual and distinct from other particulars.
For Scotus, a real, non-qualitative individual difference or “thisness” that helps constitute and explain a particular’s identity.
A nature shared by individuals of one kind; for Scotus, it has real being and less-than-numerical unity before being instantiated in particulars.
Unity that is not the numerical unity of one individual, but permits a nature to be instantiated in several individuals.
A distinction between inseparable aspects of one thing, such as its common nature and its individuating feature, without treating them as separate things.
The principle that distinct individuals must differ in some property, often understood as requiring a qualitative or relational difference.
The view that universals are primarily concepts or words rather than shared entities existing outside the mind.

questions_to_think_about: Does a property that cannot be qualitative or relational genuinely explain individuality, or does it merely rename the individual’s uniqueness?
If a common nature is real but not numerically one, what exactly is present in each of its instances?
Why might matter explain numerical difference without explaining why an individual cannot be divided into several individuals?
Is Ockham’s claim that a substance is singular through itself more economical than Scotus’s theory, or less explanatory?
Can two things be exactly alike while remaining numerically distinct?

summaries.example: Suppose two students make identical clay figures. The figures have the same shape, color, size, and position in the room. If one figure is moved, each is still a different figure. One philosopher might say their different locations now distinguish them. But before the move, Duns Scotus could say each figure had its own haecceity—a “thisness” that made it that particular figure even when their visible features matched.
summaries.summary: Medieval philosophers wondered what makes an individual individual. Duns Scotus argued that two things can share a nature—such as being human, stone, or animal—without being one and the same thing. A common nature explains their shared kind, but it does not fully explain why there are several individuals. Scotus therefore proposed haecceity, meaning “thisness.” It is a non-qualitative individual difference: not a color, size, shape, or other feature that could be shared. It helps explain why a particular is numerically one and distinct from every other particular, even if the two are exact copies. Scotus also rejected explanations based only on matter, existence, or changing qualities. Later thinkers defended or modified his view, while critics such as Ockham argued that substances are individual through themselves and that shared natures do not need Scotus’s special structure.
key_ideas: Scotus thought a shared nature explains why several things belong to one kind, but not why each one is a separate individual.
A haecceity is meant to explain individuality even when two things have exactly the same qualities.
Scotus did not describe haecceity as an empty object underneath all properties; he treated it as part of the individual.
He rejected the idea that matter, size, location, or changing qualities by themselves explain individuality.
Some opponents said that individuals are distinct through themselves, without a separate haecceity.
The disagreement is tied to a larger debate about whether common natures are real or only concepts.
summaries.why_it_matters: The question helps us separate two ideas that are easy to mix up: being the same kind of thing and being the very same individual. It also introduces a major philosophical disagreement about explanations. Some thinkers add a special feature to account for individuality; others think individuality is a basic fact. Thinking about this can sharpen how we discuss identity, copies, change, and categories.

important_terms.definition: Explaining why one object is a particular individual and why it is not another individual of the same kind.
A non-qualitative feature that makes something this individual thing rather than another matching thing.
A shared nature or essence, such as humanity, that can be found in more than one individual.
A feature that belongs to a thing because of what kind of thing it is, rather than because of an accidental change.
The numerical unity of one particular object, as opposed to a kind that can have many examples.
The view that things are individuals without needing another individualizing feature.
The medieval position that shared natures have some reality outside the mind, rather than being only names or concepts.

questions_to_think_about: Would two objects with exactly the same qualities still be two objects?
What is the difference between explaining a thing’s kind and explaining which individual it is?
If a person changes height, clothing, or location, what—if anything—makes that person the same individual?
Is a special “thisness” a useful explanation or just another word for being unique?
